doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Knowing the quartet's music was extraordinary
summary: He says he always knew Coltrane was special from hearing him with Monk, and the quartet continued that development.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: And Jack DeJohnette talks about how he had to play one set, I think you weren’t there, and then you came back and he was completely let down. He talks about that all the time, his experience with Trane. And so again Trane starts to bring more and more folks into the band, your working with this quartet and its becoming a significant force, an influential force, not only jazz but music. When did it occur to you that you were playing music that was, at that point, timeless. When we look back in history and we look at what you were doing with John Coltrane now, that obviously is music that was performed and transcended many, many of the qualities of music that we know today. When did you, as a participant in it, realize that this was far beyond anything else that was being played?

Well I always thought so cause I heard him play when they were playing with Monk. I don’t think anybody could duplicate that. And he just got better; it just expanded from that point at that little club on the Bowery. So I just thought it was a continuation of that development.
